newsitem.title: FRANCE: Party colleague sharply attacks France's Juppe.
newsitem.headline: Party colleague sharply attacks France's Juppe.

text.p: Embattled French Prime Minister Alain Juppe came under attack on Wednesday from senior party colleague Charles Pasqua, who accused him of bringing France close to collapse and the brink of revolution.
"This is 1788. French society is on the eve of rebellion," Pasqua, an ex-interior minister and anti-Maastricht campaigner, told the daily Le Monde in a reference to the 1789 French revolution.

Pasqua, who has dropped out of the limelight since he campaigned for President Jacques Chirac's fellow Gaullist rival Edouard Balladur in last year's presidential election, described Juppe as no more than an aide to Chirac.

Juppe, whose popularity has plunged amid record unemployment, has come under growing criticism from within his fractious centre-right coalition over his drive to cut the state deficit in order to join the single European currency.

But Pasqua's attack was the sharpest so far from a colleague in his own Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR) party, and RPR Secretary-General Jean-Francois Mancel condemned it as "a direct attack on the president of the Republic".
Pasqua said later on television he had made his comments in an informal chat with a journalist.

He said he had been tempted to speak out because the government was deaf, and in another angry outburst, added: "Someone aged 70 can be perfectly clear-headed while I know a few who had better retire at 50 because they are gaga and don't understand anything about the life of the French people."
Pasqua is 69 and Juppe 51.
The RPR floor leader in the National Assembly, Michel Pericard, said Pasqua's criticism reflected the opinion of only a small minority and was the mark of a sore loser.
Chirac told a cabinet meeting on Wednesday that "changing course is out of the question".

Juppe admitted to an RPR meeting on Tuesday night that the government was going through tough times. He said unemployment, at 12.6 percent and rising, was overshadowing the effect of his reforms to restore the country's finances to health.
He said he planned to keep his job and accused his opponents of demagoguery.
The leader of the Union for French Democracy (UDF) junior partner in the ruling coalition, Francois Leotard, recently urged Chirac to reshuffle the cabinet or call an early election.
Fears have been growing in the ruling coalition that social discontent may return the Socialists to power in the next general election scheduled in 1998.

Pasqua's attack came after reports earlier this week that his former fellow anti-Maastricht campaigner Philippe Seguin had drafted an alternative government platform in case Chirac decided to sack Juppe.
Seguin and Pasqua led a campaign against the Maastricht Treaty on European Monetary Union which was narrowly approved in a 1992 referendum.

The reports said Seguin, the Gaullist speaker of the National Assembly, would propose to shift emphasis from cutting deficits to fighting unemployment and push for radical interest rate cuts to revive the economy.
An opinion poll released on Wednesday said 63 percent of 937 voters questioned favoured appointing a new prime minister.
Asked who they would prefer for the job, they ranked Seguin fourth, Pasqua sixth and Juppe seventh, the survey by the polling institute Filifop said.

The top two were both Socialists: former European Commission president Jacques Delors and Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin. Ex-premier Edouard Balladur, Chirac's defeated Gaullist presidential rival, came third.
